title: The Tycoons You Envy Are Survivors: Nine in Ten Startups Don't Live to Three
dek: Xiao Lin says the common trait among big names is "guts" — the willingness to take on risk. But that's the survivor's view: nine in ten startups don't live to three years, and the risks taken by those who made it out are hidden by the spotlight.
why: Medium information density: half the episode is personal history and live Q&A. But the investment-banking promotion structure, the content production workflow, and her survivor's-eye view of "tycoons" are things you can take away.
who: Young people who want to build a personal content business or are agonizing over whether to leave a big tech company or an investment bank; practitioners curious about the internal promotion ladder at investment banks and the content production workflow.
skip: The second half of the audience Q&A starting at 30:25 repeats itself a lot; you can jump straight to the topic preview at 53:32.

points.h: Before the data drops, the trading floor goes dead silent
points.body: She says that when she was in school she couldn't make sense of financial news at all — hearing "GDP is up" she had no idea what it had to do with her; only after she started working did she feel "the real connection between the data and your job." The trading floor at an investment bank is normally very loud, loud enough that you have to shout to someone a few rows away, but before the US employment data is released the whole floor really does go dead silent, everyone staring at their screens; the moment the number comes out, client calls start coming in. What she wants her videos and her book to convey is exactly this connection: behind macro data there are stories tied to life.

points.h: Make VP, and you may stay VP for the rest of your life
points.body: Promotion at an investment bank follows a pyramid ratio: you come in as an analyst, move up to associate in about three years, then to VP in another three. VP is basically guaranteed — as long as you're not too bad and you work hard, you'll get there. But above that, director is where the culling starts; if you never get promoted, "you might be a VP for the rest of your life." Above that is managing director, a very managerial level. The rules she sums up for herself are two: first you have to have real ability and live off that ability; second, on that foundation, read the situation clearly and understand the times.

points.h: What made her dare to quit was an escape route
points.body: She agonized for about half a year before quitting to start her own thing, working her job while running a side business. The turning point was her mentor — a senior woman with a BlackRock background who had also quit to start her own company — telling her, "Just go out and do it. Worst case you do it for a year or two, and if it doesn't work you go back and find a job." She says she's actually quite conservative and risk-averse, and wants a floor under her; only when she knows there's a way back does she dare to move forward. Asked when she felt she no longer needed the escape route, she answered 2019, after the product had gotten on track in every respect.

points.h: A platform taking a 20% cut couldn't survive
points.body: She started at the end of 2017 and formally quit in mid-2018. At first she wanted to build a consulting platform: she sent cold emails to lots of people on LinkedIn looking for mentors, and being rejected and questioned was routine; when someone replied in the middle of the night she'd pick up the phone and pitch like a salesperson. In the end she onboarded one or two hundred teachers, but promotion hit a major obstacle — people wouldn't buy into paying for consulting. The platform took a 20% commission, nowhere near enough to sustain the business, and after about half a year she pivoted to education consulting services. It was only when looking for investors that she understood what they cared about was market size.

points.h: Hot topic plus story plus substance equals a hit
points.body: Her hit formula has only three parts: "hot topic plus story plus substance equals a hit." First borrow a hot topic, and ideally the hot topic is itself a story — people have been taking in lessons through stories since childhood, which is easier to accept and remember than frameworks and logic; then add substance, so people feel they got something out of it, and it spreads easily. The matching topic-selection process is to first research heavily, judge whether there's a knowledge framework in there worth extracting and whether it would be interesting to tell, then discuss it together into an outline, then refine it into a script, shoot, edit, score, and publish.

points.h: Every tycoon you see is a survivor
points.body: She sums up the common traits of big names with two words: "guts" and "substance." "Guts" because getting to that position means they took on the corresponding risk — but she stresses this isn't necessarily something everyone should chase: what we see are the most dazzling people, the ones who made it out, and "maybe 90% of startups don't live to three years"; many who took those risks died. "Substance" means being down-to-earth; people who really make it have a lot going on at the level of fundamental understanding, and the playbook of just raising money definitely won't work.

points.h: College is when trying things costs the least
points.body: She says college is a particularly good period for experimenting, because after you start working, suddenly switching careers wastes a lot of time — three years are already gone, and in another industry you have to start from scratch, whereas in college you don't pay that time cost. The real barrier to getting an internship is thick skin: when she was looking for her first internship in the US she just said she didn't need money and asked whether she could help with the work, and someone actually accepted; once you have that first foot in the door you can snowball it, starting with very small companies and applying a little higher each time. The hardest part is how to get that first entry point, so intern a lot and reach out a lot.

points.h: To analyze a big economy, enter through the timeline
points.body: Given a big topic like a whole country, her entry point is history and development: handing you a Turkey or a United States outright is too complex, but from its process of going from zero to one you can find points or patterns worth telling, and then find key nodes along the timeline for extended analysis. She says studying a company is the same: watch how it grew step by step, why it pivoted at key nodes, what the market environment was at the time, and gradually you can see clearly why it became what it is now. She also mentions that the hardest thing is finding "one line" through a pile of information and building the framework — that's more useful than memorizing details.
